strengths: Provides a clear, principled decomposition of 'zero-shot multi-resolution' inference into two interpretable sub-tasks (frequency extrapolation and resolution interpolation), grounded in classical signal-processing theory (Nyquist/aliasing), which gives a rigorous lens for diagnosing MLO failure modes.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three standard PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes) with consistent methodology, extensive hyperparameter search (detailed in appendix), and thorough ablations across many resolutions/filter limits.
Uses spectral-energy analysis (not just aggregate error metrics) to visually and quantitatively demonstrate aliasing artifacts, which is a compelling and intuitive way to expose the failure mode.

Critically evaluates two previously proposed 'fixes' (physics-informed losses, band-limited architectures like CNO/CROP) and shows neither solves the core generalization problem, adding useful negative results to the literature.

Proposes a simple, practical, and computationally cheap multi-resolution training strategy (mostly low-res + small high-res data) that empirically improves multi-resolution robustness, with a reasonable cost-accuracy tradeoff analysis (Fig. 9).
Very thorough and transparent reporting (extensive appendices with per-dataset breakdowns, loss heatmaps, training time analysis, max-mode ablations), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central empirical finding—that models trained on band-limited/fixed-resolution data cannot represent frequencies beyond their training resolution and exhibit aliasing—is a fairly direct and somewhat expected consequence of the sampling theorem and general ML out-of-distribution generalization, limiting the paper's conceptual novelty despite its polemical framing ('False Promise').

The paper's broad claims about 'machine-learned operators' are based almost entirely on FNO (with CNO/CROP only evaluated as candidate fixes, not as independently tested MLO architectures); other prominent mesh-invariant architectures (DeepONet, GNO, U-NO, etc.) are discussed in related work but never empirically tested, so the generality of the 'false promise' claim across the broader MLO class is not fully substantiated.

The proposed remedy (multi-resolution training) is conceptually simple and closely related to prior work (Li et al. 2024a's dual-resolution active learning), so the technical contribution here is more of an empirical extension/ratio study than a fundamentally new method; optimal resolution-mixing ratios are not theoretically justified and are only explored via a coarse grid.

Datasets are limited to canonical, relatively simple/synthetic PDEBench benchmarks; it is unclear how findings transfer to more complex, real-world scientific computing settings with irregular meshes, adaptive refinement, or 3D domains, which is a stated motivation of the paper.

Some presentation issues: certain figures (e.g., normalized residual energy plots) are visually dense and hard to parse quantitatively, and precise numerical comparisons (e.g., improvement magnitudes from multi-resolution training vs. zero-shot baselines) are sometimes only qualitative rather than tabulated with confidence intervals or statistical significance.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question: whether the widely-repeated claim that FNOs (and MLOs more broadly) achieve accurate zero-shot super-resolution actually holds, which has practical implications for the scientific ML community.

Provides a clean conceptual decomposition of 'multi-resolution inference' into resolution interpolation (fixed frequency content, varying sampling rate) and information extrapolation (fixed sampling rate, varying frequency content), which is a useful framing for diagnosing failure modes.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across three standard PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes) with extensive appendix material, spectral-energy diagnostics, and heatmaps of cross-resolution test loss.

Evaluates two previously proposed remedies (physics-informed losses, band-limited/alias-free architectures such as CNO and CROP) and shows neither solves the underlying generalization problem, which is a useful negative result for the field.
Proposes a practical, computationally cheap mitigation (multi-resolution training with mostly low-resolution data) and shows a favorable cost/accuracy tradeoff via a Pareto-style analysis (Fig. 9).
weaknesses: The paper's title and framing ('Machine-Learned Operators' broadly) overclaim relative to the actual scope: the central multi-resolution failure analysis (Sec. 3) is conducted almost exclusively on FNO, with CNO/CROP only tested as candidate fixes rather than as independently studied MLO architectures; other prominent operator-learning families (DeepONet, GNO, U-NO, Galerkin Transformer) are not examined at all, so generalizing the 'false promise' conclusion to MLOs as a class is not fully substantiated.

The core empirical finding—that models trained at one discretization alias/fail when tested at another due to standard Nyquist/OOD effects—is largely an expected consequence of basic signal-processing theory (which the paper itself reviews in Sec. 2); the contribution is more a careful, thorough demonstration than a conceptually novel result.

The proposed remedy (multi-resolution training) is a fairly obvious/incremental fix already foreshadowed by prior work (Li et al., 2024a, on dual-resolution active learning); the paper does not provide a principled method for choosing resolution ratios, and explicitly defers 'optimizing the ratios' to future work, weakening the completeness of the proposed solution.

Results for band-limited methods (CNO/CROP) are inconsistent across datasets (they underperform FNO on Darcy/Burgers but reportedly outperform it on Navier-Stokes, per Appendix F), yet the main text draws a fairly uniform negative conclusion about band-limited learning without fully reconciling this dataset-dependent behavior.

The benchmark PDEs (Darcy, Burgers, incompressible NS from PDEBench) are relatively simple/canonical; it is unclear how well the aliasing/multi-resolution failure conclusions transfer to more complex, real-world, or higher-dimensional scientific applications where MLOs are often deployed.

Limited theoretical contribution—the paper is purely empirical/diagnostic; no formal analysis or bound is given to characterize when/why aliasing occurs beyond restating the sampling theorem, so the work reads more as a rigorous empirical audit than a new methodological or theoretical advance.

strengths: Addresses an important, practically consequential question: whether the widely-repeated claim of 'zero-shot super-resolution' in FNOs and other machine-learned operators actually holds, providing a much-needed empirical reality check for a claim that is often taken for granted in the neural operator literature.

The conceptual decomposition of multi-resolution generalization into 'resolution interpolation' (fixed frequency content, varying sampling rate) and 'information extrapolation' (fixed sampling rate, varying frequency content) is a clean and useful framing that clarifies what is actually being tested and helps explain the observed aliasing failure modes via a clear connection to the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem.

Comprehensive experimental design spanning three standard PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes) with careful, documented hyperparameter search (grid search over learning rate/weight decay/physics loss weighting, reported in appendix tables), multiple visualizations (spectra, residual energy, heatmaps of train/test resolution loss), and extensive appendix material supporting the main claims.

The paper goes beyond simply reporting a negative result: it empirically evaluates two previously proposed remedies (physics-informed losses and band-limited/alias-free architectures such as CNO and CROP) and shows neither solves the underlying out-of-distribution generalization problem, which adds diagnostic value beyond a single dataset/method demonstration.

The proposed multi-resolution training strategy is simple, practical, and includes a thoughtful cost-accuracy analysis (Fig. 8-9, Fig. 31) showing that mixing mostly cheap low-resolution data with a small fraction of expensive high-resolution data achieves near-Pareto-optimal performance, which is actionable for practitioners.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: dataset descriptions, PDE definitions, and model implementation references (existing FNO/CNO/CROP codebases) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: aliasing and discretization-mismatch issues in mesh-invariant/band-limited neural operators have already been discussed in prior work (e.g., Bartolucci et al. 2023 on alias-free operator learning, Raonic et al. 2023 CNO, Gao et al. 2025 CROP, Li et al. 2024a dual-resolution active learning), so this paper's central empirical finding (FNOs alias when queried off their training resolution) largely corroborates rather than overturns existing understanding; the main new contribution is the systematic decoupling of interpolation/extrapolation and the breadth of the empirical sweep, which is useful but not conceptually novel.

The proposed fix (multi-resolution training) is essentially standard multi-scale/multi-resolution data augmentation, and its effectiveness is unsurprising given the paper's own OOD framing (train on the distribution you'll be tested on); there is little new methodological or theoretical insight into why or how the low-resolution-heavy mixing ratio achieves near-Pareto performance beyond an empirical sweep.

Only FNO is studied in the main failure-mode analysis (Sec. 3); while CNO/CROP are evaluated as 'corrective methods,' other prominent mesh-invariant/mesh-free architectures (e.g., DeepONet, U-NO, geometry-informed or transformer-based neural operators) are not tested, limiting the generality of the 'MLOs fail at zero-shot multi-resolution' claim implied by the title.

The evaluation of physics-informed constraints (Sec. 4.1) uses a single family of physics losses (from Li et al. 2024b) with limited weighting values (0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5) and a fairly coarse hyperparameter search; the conclusion that physics constraints 'do not enable multi-resolution generalization' may be sensitive to loss formulation, curriculum/annealing schedules, or architecture choices not explored here, so the negative result could be somewhat overstated.

No theoretical analysis or formal argument is given for why FNOs alias in the way documented (beyond citing the sampling theorem); the paper is purely empirical/diagnostic, which limits its contribution to demonstrating symptoms rather than establishing a deeper mechanistic or theoretical understanding of the failure.

Some experimental choices are not fully justified (e.g., why particular low-pass filter limits and resolution sets were chosen per dataset, or why dual-resolution training ratios were swept only up to 0.95/0.05), and the writing has minor issues (e.g., typos such as 'avaliable', some redundant phrasing) that could be tightened.

strengths: Thorough and systematic empirical decomposition of the 'zero-shot super-resolution' claim into interpolation and extrapolation sub-problems, providing a clean conceptual framework (Fig. 2) that is useful beyond this specific paper.

Extensive experimental coverage across three standard PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes) and multiple architectures (FNO, CNO, CROP+FNO, DeepONet), as well as two proposed remedies from prior work (physics-informed loss, band-limited learning), giving a comprehensive negative result rather than a single cherry-picked example.

Unusually rigorous reproducibility effort: hyperparameter grid searches, multi-seed sensitivity analysis, testing across six different hardware/software stacks, and multiple downsampling strategies (strided, average pooling, bilinear) to rule out confounds.

The proposed multi-resolution training fix is simple, practical, and shown to be computationally cheap (mostly low-resolution data with small high-resolution fraction), with a clear cost-accuracy Pareto analysis (Fig. 9) that has direct practical utility for the SciML community.
Clear, well-organized presentation with spectral-energy diagnostics that intuitively visualize the aliasing failure mode, making the argument compelling and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The core finding—that neural operators trained at one resolution do not generalize perfectly out-of-distribution to other resolutions—is somewhat expected from general ML generalization principles and is already hinted at in some of the cited literature (e.g., Bartolucci et al. 2023, Lanthaler et al. 2024); the paper's novelty lies more in systematic quantification than in a conceptually new insight.

The proposed solution (multi-resolution training) is incremental and closely related to prior multi-fidelity/multi-resolution training and active-learning approaches already cited (Li et al. 2024a, Tang et al. 2024, Lyu et al. 2023); the paper mainly extends and re-validates these ideas rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

Experiments are restricted to relatively simple, small-scale 1D/2D PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes from PDEBench); it is unclear how findings generalize to more complex, higher-dimensional, or real-world scientific simulation settings where MLOs are most valuable.

No theoretical analysis or formal characterization of why/when aliasing occurs beyond the Nyquist argument; the explanation of failure remains largely descriptive (spectral plots) rather than mechanistic.

The paper's title and framing ('false promise') is somewhat polemical relative to the modesty of the actual technical contribution, and the optimal ratio selection for multi-resolution training is left as an open/future problem rather than resolved, limiting the practical completeness of the proposed fix.

strengths: The paper carefully decomposes the amorphous notion of 'zero-shot multi-resolution inference' into two well-motivated sub-problems (resolution interpolation vs. information/frequency extrapolation), grounded in classical sampling theory (Nyquist/aliasing). This decomposition is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution for the SciML community that has often conflated these behaviors.

Empirical claims are tested across three standard PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes) and multiple architectures (FNO, CNO, CROP+FNO, DeepONet, physics-informed FNO), which is a broader sweep than most related discretization-invariance papers.

The paper goes beyond simply demonstrating failure and evaluates two previously proposed remedies (physics-informed losses, band-limited architectures), showing neither solves the underlying issue -- this is a useful negative result for practitioners choosing among existing 'fixes.'

Extensive appendix material: hyperparameter search tables, sensitivity analysis over 3 seeds, robustness checks across down-sampling procedures (strided/avg-pool/bilinear), and even a cross-hardware reproducibility study (6 different GPU/CPU/Metal backends) -- an unusually thorough reproducibility effort.

The proposed multi-resolution training solution is simple, practical, and directly actionable, with an explicit cost-accuracy tradeoff analysis (mostly-low-resolution + small high-resolution fraction) that could be immediately useful to practitioners.

The core empirical finding (spectral energy divergence beyond the training cutoff frequency, visualized via energy spectra and residual spectra) is a fairly convincing and reproducible diagnostic, not just aggregate MSE numbers.
weaknesses: The central 'false promise' framing overstates the novelty of the core finding: it is well known in the neural operator literature (and even acknowledged implicitly by works like Lanthaler et al. 2024 on FNO discretization error, and Bartolucci et al. 2023 on aliasing) that FNOs trained at one resolution do not automatically resolve frequencies beyond their training truncation. The paper's own experimental setup (low-pass filtering training data, then testing on data with genuinely new frequency content) essentially guarantees failure by construction -- this is closer to confirming a predictable consequence of finite Fourier truncation (max_modes) than to disproving a nontrivial claim.

The 'information extrapolation' experiments are somewhat tautological: an FNO with fixed number of Fourier modes m literally cannot represent frequencies above m regardless of resolution, so failing to predict frequencies beyond the training low-pass limit is close to a mathematical necessity of the architecture rather than a surprising empirical discovery. The paper's own max-mode ablation (Appendix I) confirms this but doesn't sufficiently emphasize that this specific failure is architecturally guaranteed rather than an 'emergent' generalization failure.

The original FNO zero-shot super-resolution claim (Li et al. 2020a) was primarily about interpolating to a finer discretization of the SAME underlying frequency content (i.e., mesh-invariance for fixed bandlimited signals), not about extrapolating to genuinely new high-frequency information absent from training. By testing extrapolation to new frequencies as part of the 'false promise,' the paper partly attacks a stronger claim than what was originally made, which risks strawmanning the target contribution.

The proposed 'solution' (multi-resolution training) is incremental and has already been explored in closely related forms by cited prior work (Li et al. 2024a dual-resolution active learning, Rowbottom et al. 2025, Tang et al. 2024, Lyu et al. 2023) -- the paper's contribution here is largely a systematic ratio-sweep rather than a fundamentally new technique, and this is somewhat underplayed relative to the paper's framing as a novel proposal.

No theoretical analysis or error bound is offered to characterize when/why multi-resolution training works or how much high-resolution data is 'enough' beyond empirical sweep observations; the guidance ('mostly low-res + a little high-res') is dataset/architecture specific and not clearly generalizable.

Some experimental design choices could bias conclusions in FNO's disfavor: e.g., hyperparameters (especially max_modes) are tuned once on a specific resolution and reused across resolutions rather than optimized per test scenario, and the physics-informed loss weighting/implementation may not reflect best current practice for Li et al. (2024b), potentially making the baselines look weaker than achievable.

The presentation is dense with many near-redundant figures/appendices (10 spectral plots per architecture x dataset), which, combined with the polemical title, gives the paper a somewhat one-sided, thesis-driven tone rather than a balanced scientific investigation.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical investigation across three PDE datasets (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes), multiple architectures (FNO, CNO, CROP, DeepONet), and multiple candidate fixes (physics-informed loss, band-limited learning, anti-alias nonlinearities), which gives the central claim strong empirical support.

The decomposition of 'multi-resolution inference' into resolution interpolation vs. information extrapolation is a clean and useful conceptual framework that clarifies exactly why zero-shot super-resolution fails (out-of-distribution frequency content vs. out-of-distribution sampling rate).

Exceptional reproducibility effort: hyperparameter grids, multi-seed sensitivity analysis, robustness checks across six different hardware/software stacks, and multiple downsampling strategies (strided, average pooling, bilinear), all included in appendices.

Directly challenges a widely repeated and influential claim in the neural operator literature (zero-shot super-resolution of FNO), which is of clear practical importance to the SciML community and could correct future citation/usage practices.

The proposed multi-resolution training remedy is simple, practical, and shown to be computationally cheap (mostly low-resolution data with small high-resolution fraction), with quantified memory/wall-clock savings.
Clear, well-organized writing and figures that consistently visualize spectral energy/residuals to make the aliasing phenomenon intuitive.
weaknesses: The core negative finding (that FNOs alias/fail to generalize to resolutions and frequency content outside their training distribution) is largely consistent with what is already implied by prior work on aliasing in neural operators (Bartolucci et al. 2023; Karras et al. 2021; Gao et al. 2025), somewhat limiting the novelty of the central claim beyond providing a more systematic empirical demonstration.

The proposed solution, multi-resolution training, is a fairly obvious remedy once the problem is framed as an out-of-distribution generalization issue (i.e., train on the resolutions you want to test on); it is not a substantially new methodological contribution and is closely related to existing multi-fidelity/multi-resolution training approaches cited in the paper (Li et al. 2024a, Tang et al. 2024, Lyu et al. 2023).

The physics-informed loss comparison uses a limited weighting sweep (w up to 0.5) and may not reflect a well-tuned physics-informed baseline; concluding broadly that 'physics constraints do not enable multi-resolution generalization' may be too strong given the shallow hyperparameter exploration of this baseline relative to the data-driven baseline.
No theoretical analysis or formal characterization of why/when aliasing occurs beyond the standard Nyquist argument; the contribution is purely empirical/diagnostic.

Optimal ratios for multi-resolution training (which proportions of low/high-resolution data to use) are not systematically optimized or theoretically justified beyond ad hoc sweeps; the paper acknowledges this itself as future work, leaving the practical recipe somewhat incomplete.

The datasets used (Darcy, Burgers, incompressible NS from PDEBench) are all standard, relatively simple benchmark PDEs; it's unclear how well the findings and the multi-resolution training fix would generalize to more complex, real-world, or 3D operator learning settings.
